label: Person
name: Abraham of Ephesus
summary:
Abraham of Ephesus (fl. 6th century) was a Byzantine Archbishop of Ephesus who served during the reign of Emperor Justinian I, holding one of the most historically prestigious sees in early Christianity. Ephesus had been the see of the Apostle John, the site of the Third Ecumenical Council (431), and a city of exceptional religious and cultural importance in the eastern Mediterranean.

Abraham's archiepiscopate falls within the turbulent period of Justinian's theological initiatives, when the emperor was attempting to impose religious unity across the Byzantine Empire, particularly regarding the Chalcedonian settlement and the 'Three Chapters' controversy. Ephesus's bishops were deeply embedded in the controversies of Byzantine theology, given the city's central role in the Council of Ephesus (431) that proclaimed Mary as Theotokos and condemned Nestorius.

His tenure represents the continuing prestige of the Ephesian see centuries after its founding importance, even as Constantinople's ecclesiastical influence was gradually overshadowing the older sees of Asia Minor. The sixth-century decline of Ephesus itself — from one of the Roman world's largest cities to a much smaller Byzantine provincial centre — provides the backdrop to his archiepiscopate.
